outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the first open case of the conjecture, (k,ℓ) = (6,4), has been settled by a single-author preprint (Bonnet, submitted 19 Aug 2026, threshold 10¹¹⁰⁵⁵⁹³¹; the author says the detailed proof was supplied by GPT-5.6 Sol Pro). A later single-author note (Cambie, 17 Sep 2026) gives the same (6,4) conclusion with threshold 880 and credits GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 with assistance. Bhattacharya et al. (22 Sep 2026) prove a four-collinear-or-K₇∖e statement, which they say comes within one visibility edge of (7,4), and they credit GPT-6 Astra with the initial proofs of two theorems. Sarkar (30 Apr 2026) gives quantitative results only for structured point sets. The statement for all pairs (k,ℓ) remains open, and no event in the window bears on any other pair.
problem_asks: The statement, unpacked: (1) for every pair of positive integers k and ℓ there exists an integer n(k,ℓ), so the claim is one existence statement per pair; (2) for every finite point set P in the plane R² with at least n(k,ℓ) points, P contains ℓ collinear points or k pairwise visible points, where two points are visible when no third point of P lies on the open segment between them, so that the visibility graph of P has a clique of size k; (3) the sets are finite (the claim fails for infinite sets, Pór and Wood 2010); (4) the points lie in the plane (the literature notes that the statement is equivalent when stated in R^d for any d ≥ 2, which I did not verify). The Wikipedia wording 'many collinear points or many mutually visible points' is loose; the parts above are the literature's form, Kára–Pór–Wood's Conjecture 1. The trivial cases are ℓ ≤ 3 (no three collinear makes the visibility graph complete) and k ≤ 2. Earlier results settle k ≤ 4 for every ℓ (Kára–Pór–Wood, per secondary sources) and k = 5 for every ℓ (Abel et al. 2009, with (5,4) earlier by Addario-Berry et al.). The statement as a whole is settled only if every remaining pair with k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4 is handled.

events.what_happened: Ján Kára, Attila Pór and David R. Wood posed the big-line-big-clique conjecture as Conjecture 1 of their paper on the chromatic number of visibility graphs (Discrete & Computational Geometry 34(3), 2005, pp. 497–506, per a search summary; a Charles University preprint dates from 2004). Secondary sources (Open Problem Garden snippet, Pór and Wood 2010, Abel et al. 2009 citation trail, and search summaries) report that they proved the case k ≤ 4 for every ℓ. The original text was not read, so the k ≤ 4 claim is secondary-sourced only.
events.revisions: Charles University KAM preprint series 2004 (not opened); Discrete & Computational Geometry 34(3) 2005 per search summary (listing not opened).
events.delivers: Posed the conjecture and, per secondary sources, proves it for k ≤ 4 and every ℓ. The ℓ ≤ 3 case is trivial.
events.remains: All pairs with k ≥ 5 and ℓ ≥ 4, and the finite-set statement for k ≥ 5 as a whole.

checked_by.who: Discrete & Computational Geometry (Springer), journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the 2005 paper, per a search summary; DOI listing appeared in search results but was not opened

events.direction: The k ≤ 4 cases go in the direction the conjecture asserts: existence of n(k,ℓ).

events.what_happened: Florian Pfender, 'On Visibility Graphs of Point Sets in the Plane' (arXiv math/0510467, v1 21 Oct 2005; Discrete & Computational Geometry 39(1):455–459, 2008, per a search summary). Shows that every graph G is realised as an induced subgraph of the visibility graph of some point set X together with the integer lattice, and as a consequence gives visibility graphs with clique number six and arbitrarily large chromatic number. This settles a question of Kára, Pór and Wood about whether chromatic number is bounded in terms of clique number. It does not involve collinear points.
events.revisions: Journal version DCG 39(1) 2008 per search summary (not opened).
events.delivers: A chromatic-number question about visibility graphs: chromatic number is unbounded with clique number fixed at six. This is a different question from the statement, which concerns collinear points together with a visible clique of size k.
events.remains: The whole statement; this event does not touch the (k,ℓ) claim.

checked_by.who: Discrete & Computational Geometry, journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper, per a search summary (not opened)

events.direction: Cuts against a chromatic-number version of the conjecture (chromatic number bounded by a function of clique number). It is not a counterexample to the collinear-plus-clique statement.
events.object: Constructive: for every graph G a finite point set X whose visibility structure with the lattice induces G on X (per the arXiv abstract). Taking G with clique number six gives visibility graphs of arbitrarily large chromatic number.

events.what_happened: Louigi Addario-Berry, Cristina Fernandes, Yoshiharu Kohayakawa, Jos Coelho de Pina and Yoshiko Wakabayashi, 'On a geometric Ramsey-style problem' (2007, as cited in Abel et al. 2009 and in search summaries). Reported as proving the statement for k = 5 and ℓ = 4. The paper was not located in two targeted searches, so this event rests entirely on secondary citations. The publication type and venue are not established.
events.revisions: Not located. 'preprint' is a placeholder to satisfy the enum; the venue is unverified.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources only: the statement for k = 5 with ℓ = 4. Not verified against the paper.
events.remains: k = 5 with ℓ ≥ 5 (later covered by Abel et al.), and all k ≥ 6.
events.doubts: The paper was not read, so its claim and proof cannot be checked from this record.
events.direction: If the secondary sources are right, the result goes in the direction the conjecture asserts (existence of n(5,4)).

events.what_happened: Zachary Abel, Brad Ballinger, Prosenjit Bose, Sébastien Collette, Vida Dujmović, Ferran Hurtado, Scott D. Kominers, Stefan Langerman, Attila Pór and David R. Wood, 'Every Large Point Set contains Many Collinear Points or an Empty Pentagon' (arXiv:0904.0262, v1 1 Apr 2009, v2 24 Apr 2009). Proves that for every integer ℓ ≥ 2, every sufficiently large planar point set contains ℓ collinear points or an empty pentagon. The abstract, as fetched, says this settles the next open case of the big-line-big-clique conjecture. Since the vertices of an empty convex pentagon are pairwise visible (the hull contains no other point), this gives the k = 5 case for every ℓ. That inference is mine; secondary sources state the k = 5 result directly.
events.revisions: v2 24 Apr 2009. Preliminary version at CCCG 2009, pp. 99–102; journal version Graphs and Combinatorics 27(1):47–60, dated 2011 by one search summary and 2010 by another (listing not opened).
events.delivers: The statement for k = 5 and every ℓ ≥ 2. The threshold is doubly exponential in ℓ per a secondary source (later improved by Barát et al. 2012).
events.remains: All pairs with k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4, and every k ≥ 6.

checked_by.who: Graphs and Combinatorics, journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the journal version, per a search summary (journal listing not opened)

events.direction: Goes in the direction the conjecture asserts: existence for k = 5.

events.what_happened: Attila Pór and David R. Wood, 'The Big-Line-Big-Clique Conjecture is False for Infinite Point Sets' (arXiv:1008.2988, v1 18 Aug 2010). Constructs a countably infinite planar point set with no four collinear points and no three pairwise visible points, so the statement fails once finiteness is dropped.
events.delivers: For infinite point sets the statement is false. It says nothing about finite sets, so this is a scope fact: the finiteness requirement is essential to the statement.
events.remains: The finite statement for every pair (k,ℓ) is unaffected.
events.direction: Counterexample to an infinite-set version. It does not contradict the finite statement.
events.object: A countably infinite planar point set with no four collinear points and no three pairwise visible points (described in the abstract; the construction itself was not read).

events.what_happened: János Barát, Vida Dujmović, Gwenaël Joret, Michael S. Payne, Ludmila Scharf, Daria Schymura, Pavel Valtr and David R. Wood, 'Empty pentagons in point sets with collinearities' (arXiv:1207.3633, v1 16 Jul 2012; SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics 29(1):198–209, 2015, per a search summary). Proves that every finite planar point set of at least 328k² points contains an empty pentagon or k collinear points, and the (k−1)×(k−1) grid shows this quadratic order is optimal up to a constant. The fetched abstract does not mention the big-line-big-clique conjecture. An Open Problem Garden comment (search snippet only) says it improves the k = 5 case.
events.delivers: A quantitative bound: the empty-pentagon-or-ℓ-collinear threshold is at most 328ℓ². Since an empty pentagon gives a visible 5-clique (my inference), this moves an upper bound on the threshold of the statement for k = 5. The (5,ℓ) status was already settled by Abel et al.; this changes a bound, not the status.
events.remains: k ≥ 6 for all ℓ ≥ 4, as before.

checked_by.who: SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics, journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper, per a search summary (not opened)

events.direction: Moves an upper bound on the threshold in the direction the conjecture asserts, for k = 5. The grid example is a lower-bound construction for the empty-pentagon threshold, not a counterexample to the conjecture.
events.object: The (k−1)×(k−1) grid, which has neither an empty pentagon nor k collinear points (per the abstract). It shows the quadratic order is optimal up to a constant.

events.what_happened: Bálint Hujter and Sándor Kisfaludi-Bak, '5 Colorable Visibility Graphs Have Bounded Size or 4 Collinear Points' (arXiv:1410.7273, v1 27 Oct 2014). Shows that any finite planar point set with at least 2311 points has four collinear points or a visibility graph that cannot be 5-coloured. The fetched abstract frames this as a relaxation of the conjecture in the chromatic direction. Per the paper as reported in search summaries, the clique statement was then open for all k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4.
events.delivers: A chromatic relaxation: at ℓ = 4, a large visibility graph cannot be 5-coloured. It does not produce a visible clique of any size, so it decides no (k,ℓ) pair of the statement.
events.remains: The clique statement for k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4 (as the paper describes it).
events.direction: A relaxation in a chromatic direction. Its conclusion is consistent with the statement but it does not establish any clique claim.

events.what_happened: Sophie Leuchtner, Carlos M. Nicolás and Andrew Suk, 'A note on visible islands' (arXiv:2109.00022, v1 31 Aug 2021; Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica 59(2):160–163, 2022, per a search summary). Shows that the statement fails for visible islands (subsets whose convex hulls contain no other point of the set, with pairwise visible points). They replace each point of a Horton set by a collinear triple, obtaining arbitrarily large planar sets with no four collinear points and no visible island of size 13.
events.revisions: arXiv URL with a v3 suffix appeared in search results (version history not opened). Journal per search summary.
events.delivers: A different variant, visible islands, is false. The construction is for the island variant and does not touch the original statement.
events.remains: The original statement for all (k,ℓ), which this event leaves untouched.

checked_by.who: Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica, journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the note, per a search summary (not opened)

events.directly_checkable: Planar point sets from a Horton set with each point replaced by a collinear triple; not checked by this pass, since only the abstract was read
events.direction: Against the visible-island variant. It does not contradict the original statement, which the abstract does not claim to refute.
events.object: Arbitrarily large finite planar point sets with no four collinear points and no visible island of size 13, obtained by replacing each point of a Horton set with a triple of collinear points.

events.what_happened: Sohail Sarkar, 'Visibility cliques, cubic containers, and dense orchard cores' (arXiv:2605.00918, v1 30 Apr 2026; math.CO, cross-listed math.MG; 18 pages, 1 figure). Single author. The paper's notation writes k for the number of collinear points, which corresponds to ℓ in the statement. Its results are: (i) if all but s points of an n-point set with no k collinear points lie on one real cubic, the set has a visible clique of size Ω_k(n/(s+1)), unless the cubic is a union of three lines; (ii) with few ordinary lines (via the Green–Tao structure theorem), a visible clique of size Ω_{k,K}(n), and all but O_K(1) points partition into O_{k,K}(1) mutually visible sets; (iii) for point sets on any fixed irreducible algebraic curve (cubic-container theorem combined with the Elekes–Szabó theorem), the big-line-big-clique conclusion holds; (iv) a dense-orchard core lemma; (v) a 'sharp example' showing ambient blockers cannot be ignored. The abstract says the paper 'isolate[s] a structural obstruction to the full conjecture'. The AI-use section says 'AI-assisted tools were used for LaTeX typesetting, literature search, and proofreading' without naming a system.
events.revisions: v1 only, as of the fetch.
events.delivers: Quantitative and structured-case results. For the point sets of the types listed in (i)–(iii), the visible clique grows with n. Result (iii) applies only to points on one fixed irreducible curve. The paper does not cover general planar point sets.
events.remains: General planar point sets, and the full statement for all (k,ℓ). The structural obstruction the paper isolates was not read in full.
events.time_since_posted: about 5.4 months (164 days) as of 11 Oct 2026
events.direction: Supports the conclusion of the statement within the structured regimes it treats. The paper states that it isolates an obstruction to the full statement, so it does not settle the general case.
events.object: The paper's 'sharp example' is a one-blocker configuration showing that ambient blockers cannot be ignored. Its construction was not read.

events.what_happened: Édouard Bonnet, 'Large Finite Point Sets Have 4 Collinear Points or a 6-Clique' (arXiv:2608.19468, v1 submitted 19 Aug 2026; 7 pages; math.CO, cs.DM). Single author; the author's homepage gives a CNRS research position at LIP, ENS Lyon. Proves that every finite planar point set of size at least 10¹¹⁰⁵⁵⁹³¹ contains four collinear points or six pairwise visible points (Theorem 1), and states that this resolves the first open case of the Kára–Pór–Wood conjecture. The AI-use section of the HTML version states: 'After one fruitless attempt and the now customary generic encouragement, a relatively detailed proof of Theorem 1 was provided by GPT-5.6 Sol Pro after pondering for 222 minutes.' It also states that 'The author's contributions were limited to checking the proof, simplifying some parts, and eventually writing the paper.' These sentences were read through a summarising fetch of the HTML rendering, which was consistent across two fetches but was not compared with the PDF.
events.revisions: v1 only, as of the fetch; no later versions listed.
events.delivers: The (k,ℓ) = (6,4) case: every finite planar point set of size at least 10¹¹⁰⁵⁵⁹³¹ has four collinear points or six pairwise visible points. Restricted to the single pair (6,4), with a qualitative threshold of astronomical size.
events.remains: Every other pair with k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4, including (6,ℓ) for ℓ ≥ 5 and (k,4) for k ≥ 7. The next open case named in later work is (7,4). The pairs with k ≤ 5, and ℓ ≤ 3, were settled earlier.

checked_by.qualification: Combinatorialist; PhD from Radboud University, per his homepage as summarised in a search result
checked_by.what_they_did: Posted a three-page note giving the same (6,4) conclusion with threshold 880, with the comment 'Improvement on [2608.19468]'. This is a shorter proof that builds on the result, not a stated verification of Bonnet's argument.

checked_by.who: Bhaswar B. Bhattacharya, Sandip Das, Sk Samim Islam, Aashirwad Mohapatra and Saumya Sen
checked_by.qualification: Authors of a 2026 combinatorics preprint. Bhattacharya is listed with the Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata in a 2011 paper's header (search snippet); the other four were not checked
checked_by.what_they_did: Restate Bonnet's stability lemma as their Lemma A.1, citing Bonnet's Lemma 2, and use its colouring inputs to get a threshold of 2·10¹³. No explicit verification statement found.

events.time_since_posted: about 7.5 weeks (53 days) as of 11 Oct 2026
events.direction: Proves the conjectured conclusion for the pair (6,4), with a qualitative threshold. This is consistent with the statement, which asserts existence of n(6,4).

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Sol Pro
systems.what_it_did: By the author's account, produced 'a relatively detailed proof of Theorem 1' (the (6,4) theorem), after one unsuccessful attempt. The author then checked the proof, simplified parts of it and wrote the paper.
systems.basis_quote: After one fruitless attempt and the now customary generic encouragement, a relatively detailed proof of Theorem 1 was provided by GPT-5.6 Sol Pro after pondering for 222 minutes.

ai.disclosed_cost: 222 minutes of model thinking time, as the author states. No token or monetary figure was found.

events.what_happened: Stijn Cambie, 'Four collinear points or six visible points' (arXiv:2609.21035, v1 submitted 17 Sep 2026; 3 pages, 1 figure). Single author. Proves that every finite planar set of at least 880 points contains four collinear points or six pairwise visible points (N(4,6) ≤ 880). The comments field says 'Improvement on [2608.19468]' and 'Not to be published; a 2 page AI version was essentially reviewed by the author.' The proof uses Hujter and Kisfaludi-Bak's Theorem 15, which relies on h(6) = 30 from Heule and Scheucher's computer-assisted result. That is a SAT-based computation and not an AI system. It also uses a clique-building lemma after Bollobás and Nikiforov. The acknowledgements say Marius Tiba presented the visibility problem at a MATRIX–MFO workshop, and that 'the bound and proof were developed through successive revisions with assistance from GPT-5.6 and GPT-6'. The full sentence was read only through a summarising fetch and a search snippet, so the wording of this phrase is the only part confirmed in two places.
events.revisions: v1 only, as of the fetch.
events.delivers: The (6,4) case again, with a finite threshold: every finite planar set of at least 880 points contains four collinear points or six pairwise visible points. This lowers the upper bound on n(6,4) from Bonnet's value and adds no new pair (k,ℓ).
events.remains: The same pairs as Bonnet's event: every pair with k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4 other than (6,4).
events.doubts: (a) Threshold gap. 880 is far below the two bounds in Bhattacharya et al. (2·10¹³ in Corollary A.2 and 7·10¹⁰ in Remark A.3), which build on Bonnet's stability inputs. That paper says 'we became aware of a new arXiv preprint [5] which establishes that 880 points suffice for the same conclusion'. It does not say that it checked Cambie's argument. (b) The author states that the bound and proof were developed with AI assistance, the paper is single-author, and the comments say it is 'Not to be published'. No independent verification was found, and no specific error was identified in any source. The competing reading is that the gap reflects a more efficient direct argument, one that makes use of the h(6) = 30 SAT result, rather than a flaw.
events.direction: The same direction as Bonnet: proves the (6,4) conclusion, with a much smaller threshold.

events.what_happened: Bhaswar B. Bhattacharya, Sandip Das, Sk Samim Islam, Aashirwad Mohapatra and Saumya Sen, 'Large Planar Point Sets Contain 4 Collinear Points or Almost 7-Cliques, and Related Results' (arXiv:2609.25727, v1 submitted 22 Sep 2026; 14 pages, 1 figure). Read from a summarising fetch of the HTML rendering: Theorem 1.1: for any fixed graph H with χ(H) ≤ 5 there is N_H such that every planar point set of size at least N_H has four collinear points or a copy of H in its visibility graph. Theorem 1.3: the same for H with χ(H) = 6 that has a colour-critical edge. Corollary 1.4: four collinear points or a copy of K₇∖e (seven points with at most one non-visible pair). Appendix: Corollary A.2 gives threshold 2·10¹³ for four collinear points or six pairwise visible points; Remark A.3 derives 7·10¹⁰ from the stability constant and the h(6) = 30 bound. The paper describes its result as coming 'within one visibility edge of' the open case (7,4). The AI declaration (Section 1.2) says 'GPT-6 Astra produced the initial proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 through a series of iterative exchanges with the authors' and 'The authors assume responsibility for all content'.
events.revisions: v1 only, as of the fetch.
events.delivers: Four collinear points or K₇∖e, which is seven points with at most one non-visible pair; the generalised statement for any fixed H with χ(H) ≤ 5, or with χ(H) = 6 and a colour-critical edge; and a threshold for the (6,4) pair (2·10¹³ in Corollary A.2, 7·10¹⁰ in Remark A.3). Restrictions: four collinear points is fixed at ℓ = 4 throughout; K₇∖e is not K₇, so no seven-clique is obtained; the (6,4) threshold is a bound on a pair already settled by Bonnet and Cambie.
events.remains: The seven-clique case (7,4), which the paper itself names as the next open case; every pair with ℓ ≥ 5 and k ≥ 6; and the full statement for all (k,ℓ).
events.direction: For the (6,4) pair, it reproves the conclusion (my inference: Theorem 1.3 applied to H = K₆, which has χ = 6 and every edge colour-critical, would cover it; the paper's text read here does not state this). For (7,4), it is a near miss and does not settle the pair. Overall, it extends the conclusion to further graphs H but adds no new (k,ℓ) pair.

systems.name: GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: By the authors' declaration (paraphrased in the HTML read), produced the initial proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 through iterative exchanges with the authors; the authors then revised the arguments and added details and examples. The paper does not say whether this is a released or an internal build.
systems.basis_quote: GPT-6 Astra produced the initial proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 through a series of iterative exchanges with the authors.

disputes.summary: The sources disagree about how much of the statement remains open. Abel et al. (2009) and the Open Problem Garden give k = 6 or ℓ = 4 as open; Hujter and Kisfaludi-Bak (2014) say open for all k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4; Bhattacharya et al. (2026) say it was open for all k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4 until Bonnet and name (7,4) as the next case. The Wikipedia article, as fetched, says the conjecture is still open in general. Its reported last edit date is 29 Jan 2026, before Bonnet's and the later preprints, so the article may simply not have been updated. The threshold figures also disagree across sources for the same (6,4) pair: 10¹¹⁰⁵⁵⁹³¹ (Bonnet), 880 (Cambie), and 2·10¹³ and 7·10¹⁰ (Bhattacharya et al.). None of these is a priority dispute, but the later pass should note that 880 is the smallest published (6,4) threshold found.

summary: Searches (39 WebSearch queries, listed below) turned up one cluster of 2026 activity on this conjecture and a set of older results. In the window since 26 January 2024 there are four events: Sarkar (arXiv 2605.00918, 30 Apr 2026), Bonnet (arXiv 2608.19468, 19 Aug 2026), Cambie (arXiv 2609.21035, 17 Sep 2026) and Bhattacharya et al. (arXiv 2609.25727, 22 Sep 2026). Each was opened through its arXiv abstract and HTML rendering. The PDFs could not be decoded by the fetch tool, and I did not read the full texts of the older papers. Bonnet proves the (6,4) case with threshold 10¹¹⁰⁵⁵⁹³¹, which is a qualitative result for one pair. The author states that the detailed proof of Theorem 1 was provided by GPT-5.6 Sol Pro after 222 minutes of pondering, and that the author's own contribution was checking, simplifying and writing up. That is a load-bearing AI attribution in the authors' own words, and it is recorded as such. Cambie gives the same (6,4) conclusion with threshold 880 in a three-page note, which the comments describe as 'Not to be published' and which credits GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 with assistance in developing the bound and the proof. The phrase is quoted from a summarising fetch and a search snippet, and it does not say which model did which step. The 880 figure is far below the two bounds in Bhattacharya et al. (2·10¹³ and 7·10¹⁰), which build on Bonnet's stability inputs and state that they became aware of the 880 result without saying they checked it. That gap is the main close call on the threshold. Bhattacharya et al. also credit GPT-6 Astra with the initial proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 and prove a four-collinear-or-K₇∖e statement, which is a near miss for (7,4) and not a settlement of it. Sarkar's April preprint gives quantitative results for structured point sets (cubic curves, few ordinary lines, fixed algebraic curves) and says it isolates an obstruction to the full conjecture; it names no AI system, only 'AI-assisted tools' for typesetting, literature search and proofreading, so it counts as AI involvement that is peripheral, not load-bearing. Nobody has verified any of the 2026 proofs publicly as far as I could find: no journal publication, no referee report, no expert blog post, no Tao or Quanta coverage, no Lean formalisation (the Lean search returned none), and no entry on erdosproblems.com (not opened directly). The OpenAI Astra announcement of 2 August 2026 (ten results, per SiliconANGLE, which I opened) lists nothing about collinear points or visibility, so Bonnet's GPT-5.6 Sol Pro result is not among the Astra announcement's results. Press reports of an 'internal version of Astra' in August 2026 are press, not authors, so I have not used them to classify any system. The older events are dated from their arXiv v1 pages where I opened them, and from search summaries for journal listings I did not open: Kára–Pór–Wood 2004 (k ≤ 4, secondary only), Pfender 2005 (a chromatic question, a different problem), Addario-Berry et al. 2007 (k = 5, ℓ = 4, not located, secondary only), Abel et al. 2009 (k = 5 for all ℓ, the abstract says it settles the next open case), Pór and Wood 2010 (false for infinite sets, a scope fact), Barát et al. 2012 (a quadratic threshold for the empty-pentagon version, which moves the k = 5 bound but not the status), Hujter and Kisfaludi-Bak 2014 (a chromatic relaxation), and Leuchtner, Nicolás and Suk 2021 (the visible-island variant is false). None of the older events falls in the window, and no event in the window touches any pair other than (6,4) and the quantitative structured-case results. Close calls, both sides: whether a single settled pair counts as progress on a statement quantified over all (k,ℓ) (I record it as partial); whether the 880 bound should be trusted given its gap to the other two (I record both readings); and whether the Cambie AI phrase is load-bearing or only assistance (the source does not say, so the later pass decides from the record).
competing_reading: Read the statement as quantified over all pairs (k,ℓ). Then one settled pair, (6,4), with a threshold of 10¹¹⁰⁵⁵⁹³¹ or 880, leaves the statement open, and the record's outcome stands. Read Bhattacharya et al.'s 'within one visibility edge' remark, and the presence of several 2026 preprints in a few weeks, as a sign that the frontier has almost closed; the paper itself still calls (7,4) open. Read the 880 bound as unreliable because of its gap to 2·10¹³ and 7·10¹⁰, and (6,4) then rests only on Bonnet, a single-author preprint whose central proof the author attributes to a model and whose checking is a single author's. Read Bonnet's 'relatively detailed proof' sentence as a model producing the whole argument, not assistance, and the AI involvement is load-bearing and direct. Read the Cambie phrase as mere assistance and the AI involvement is weaker, though the source does not say which.
what_would_settle_it: For the statement: a settled case beyond (6,4), such as (7,4) or (6,5), or a counterexample to the general conjecture. For (6,4): peer-reviewed publication of Bonnet's or Cambie's note, a named expert's written verification, or a Lean formalisation with no sorry. For the threshold gap: the authors of 2609.25727 explaining how their 7·10¹⁰ and 2·10¹³ compare with Cambie's 880, or an independent check of Cambie's argument. For the AI attribution: the authors' statement of which model did which step in Cambie's paper, and whether the 'GPT-6 Astra' and 'GPT-6' names refer to released or internal builds. For Sarkar: the full text of the structural obstruction, which was not read.

incomplete: (1) The PDFs of 2608.19468, 2609.21035, 2609.25727 and 2605.00918, and the author's PDF copy, could not be decoded by the fetch tool. Every theorem statement and AI sentence here comes from an HTML rendering read through a summarising fetch, and quotes were checked across two fetches only for the Bonnet AI sentence and the Cambie phrase. None of the proofs was read line by line, and I did not verify any proof. (2) The Cambie AI sentence was seen only as the phrase 'developed through successive revisions with assistance from GPT-5.6 and GPT-6', from a search snippet and a fetch; the full sentence was not confirmed. (3) Addario-Berry et al. 2007 was not located, so that event is secondary-sourced only. (4) The original Kára–Pór–Wood text was not read; the k ≤ 4 claim is secondary-sourced. (5) Journal listings for Abel et al., Barát et al., Pfender, Kára–Pór–Wood and Leuchtner et al. came from search summaries and were not opened. (6) The older papers were read at the abstract level only, so their AI fields rest on the abstract and not on acknowledgements. (7) Sohail Sarkar's and the other Bhattacharya co-authors' qualifications were not established. (8) Cambie's qualification is taken from a homepage summary in a search result; the homepage was not opened directly. (9) The Wikipedia article was read through a cached fetch; its displayed state may differ from the live page. The Open Problem Garden page was seen only in snippets. (10) The arXiv versions were checked only as shown on the abstract pages at the time of the fetch; later versions may exist. (11) No check was made for author replies, comments, or later versions after 11 Oct 2026.
